key_insight: IELSM replaces empirical lattice elements with a theoretically admissible polygonal spring formulation that delivers isotropic elasticity and fracture simulation on arbitrary tessellations.
engineering_relevance: It enables efficient quasi-brittle fracture modeling for concrete, rock, ceramics, composites, and masonry while simplifying FEM coupling through direct node sharing.
method: Discretize continua into polygonal cells with axial springs plus a volumetric constraint to enforce isotropic elasticity.
Derive admissible element shapes from governing equations, extending beyond classical tessellable LSM geometries.
Couple IELSM with an isotropic damage model and optionally restrict it to damage-prone regions while the rest is modeled by FEM.
evidence_signal: Benchmarks including a pure bending test and four fracture cases showed good agreement with experiments, preserved displacement accuracy, and improved efficiency, including 41.2-80.9% fewer nodes and 34.2-85.2% lower CPU time versus full-domain IELSM in coupled runs.
watch_item: Element admissibility and damage calibration depend on the theoretical constraints and constitutive model, so implementation must ensure the chosen polygonal mesh satisfies the IELSM criteria.
paper_title: Tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model for Quasi-Brittle Fracture
